docs.title: AEGISS
docs.text:
Atomic Orbital and Entropy based Guided Inference for Space Selection

AEGISS is a semi-automated protocol for defining active spaces for multireference quantum chemistry (CASSCF, CASPT2, NEVPT2) and hybrid classical–quantum calculations. It unifies the two established families of active-space selection: a correlated DMRG calculation supplies per-orbital entanglement information (in the spirit of AutoCAS), while an AVAS-like projection onto user-specified atomic orbitals extracts the chemically meaningful subset. An orbital enters the final space only when it is both strongly correlated and chemically aligned with the process of interest.

If you use AEGISS, please cite the AEGISS paper and the work it builds on (DMRG, block2, AVAS, the single-orbital entropy, PySCF and ASE); see Citing AEGISS.

docs.title: The AEGISS procedure
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    G([Input geometry]) --> S1
    subgraph pre [Pre-processing]
        S1[1 · Atom labeling]
        S4[4 · Desired AO labels]
    end
    S1 --> S2[2 · Mean-field<br/>HF · KS · ΔSCF · embedding]
    S2 --> S3[3 · DMRG +<br/>orbital-entropy screening]
    S3 --> S5[5 · AO projection on<br/>entropy-selected MOs]
    S4 --> S5
    S5 --> S6([6 · Active space])

Following Section 3 of the AEGISS paper, the workflow proceeds in six steps.

docs.title: 1 · Atom labeling — pre-processing, optional
docs.text: The molecule is partitioned into clusters \(C_i\); each atom \(X\) in cluster \(i\) is labeled \(X_i\), and the union of clusters defines the full set \(\{R\}\). A coarse labeling gives a general description, a finer one targets specific atomic orbitals. Skip this step if you have no prior knowledge of the system. See also MolTagger for interactive tagging.

docs.title: 2 · Mean-field calculation
docs.text: An HF (or Kohn–Sham DFT) SCF yields the MO coefficient matrix \([C]_{\mu p}\); an embedding framework (e.g. solvation) can be included here. If the process of interest is localized, an active region \(A\) is identified and only its orbitals \(\{\psi^A_p\}\) are retained — the environment is left untouched and every subsequent step operates within \(A\).

docs.title: 3 · Single-orbital entropy screening
docs.text:
A correlated wavefunction (approximate DMRG) is computed inside \(A\) and used to build each orbital's one-orbital reduced density matrix \(\rho^p\). The single-orbital entropy

\[ S(1)_p = -\sum_{\alpha=1}^{4} \omega_{\alpha,p} \ln \omega_{\alpha,p} \]

(with \(\{\omega_{\alpha,p}\}\) the eigenvalues of \(\rho^p\)) ranks orbitals by entanglement. All orbitals with \(S(1)_p > \tau_E = S(1)_{\max}/10\) are retained. In practice, choose the active region \(N_A\) as a Fermi-level window a few times larger than the expected final CAS and check that the highly entropic orbitals lie well inside it.

The window is taken by orbital index (ncas orbitals around the occupied/virtual boundary), which follows the Fermi level only for canonical orbitals, ordered by orbital energy. Localized orbitals (Boys, Pipek–Mezey, Edmiston–Ruedenberg, IBOs) are obtained by rotating the occupied and virtual blocks separately: the occupied/virtual partition is preserved, but localized orbitals have no orbital energies, so their order within each block is arbitrary and an index window over them is no longer a frontier window. Natural orbitals are ordered by occupation number instead, a different but still meaningful criterion. Localization can be combined with AEGISS, but then check explicitly that the window contains the orbitals of interest.

docs.title: 4 · Atomic-orbital selection
docs.text: Chemically relevant AOs are identified from prior chemical knowledge: for each cluster label \(X_i\) an AO type is specified (e.g. "C 2pz", "Fe 3d"), forming combined labels that are grouped into one or more AO sets \(D \in \mathcal{D}\).

docs.title: 5 · Atomic-orbital projection
docs.text: Following AVAS, an auxiliary minimal atomic-orbital basis (MinAO) is built and, for each group \(D\), overlapped against the entropy-selected active-region MOs. Orbitals are then kept either by a contribution threshold \(\epsilon_D\) or by top-N ranking on the resulting projection weights \(w_p^D\).

docs.title: 6 · Active space
docs.text:
The per-group selections are merged into the final active space

\[ \{\psi_r\} = \bigcup_{D \in \mathcal{D}} \{\psi_r^D\}, \]

refined further if required. The result is applicable to both classical CAS-based methods and hybrid classical–quantum calculations.

Note

The tutorials walk through each step with runnable notebooks and give the full mathematical treatment.

docs.title: When to use AEGISS
docs.text:
AEGISS is built for ground-state active spaces where you know, or can guess, which atomic orbitals matter: it keeps an orbital only when it is both strongly correlated and aligned with those AOs. It is deliberately conservative, so inspect the result, especially for orbital mixing and Rydberg-like virtuals. These are poor fits:

  • Reaction paths: not tested. Check each geometry's selection by hand.
  • Excited states with no counterpart in the ground state: the DMRG is run on the ground state, so such orbitals are not seen. AEGISS has no remedy for this: choose those orbitals by hand or with another method.
  • No idea which atomic orbitals matter: the AO step then has nothing to work with and AEGISS reduces to entropy alone (AutoCAS), or to its AVAS-like limit without clusters. Use an entropy-only selection (AutoCAS).
  • Localized orbitals as input: the DMRG window is a Fermi-level index window and localized orbitals have no orbital energies. Start from canonical or natural orbitals.
  • Essentially single-reference systems (S(1)max small, every orbital weakly correlated): no active space is needed, as CCSD, CISD or DFT are already reasonable.

How to choose the window, thresholds and labels is on the Choosing parameters page.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
from aegiss.initial_guess import build_mol, run_scf
from aegiss.active_space import select_aegiss
from aegiss.config_dataclasses import DMRGConfig, EntropyConfig, ProjectionConfig, OutputConfig

mol = build_mol("molecule.xyz", basis="ccpvdz")
mf  = run_scf(mol, method="RHF")

active_indices = select_aegiss(
    mol, mf,
    dmrg_config=DMRGConfig(ncas=20, nelecas=20, symm_type="SZ"),
    entropy_config=EntropyConfig(fraction=0.1, fraction_type="r", ranking="global"),
    projection_config=ProjectionConfig(ao_labels=["C 2pz"], contribution=0.5),
    output_config=OutputConfig(saving_folder="./orbs/"),
)

docs.title: Methods AEGISS builds on
docs.text:
AEGISS ranks orbitals by their single-orbital entropy from a DMRG calculation, run with block2, and combines that with an AVAS-like projection onto atomic orbitals. It is built on PySCF, and MolTagger uses ASE. Please also cite the papers behind them.

  • S. R. White, Density-matrix algorithms for quantum renormalization groups, Phys. Rev. B 48, 10345 (1993). doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.48.10345
  • G. K.-L. Chan and M. Head-Gordon, Highly correlated calculations with a polynomial cost algorithm: A study of the density matrix renormalization group, J. Chem. Phys. 116, 4462 (2002). doi:10.1063/1.1449459

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Bug reports, feature requests, documentation fixes and code are all welcome. Open issues with the issue templates and read the contributing guide, the Code of Conduct and the Contributor License Agreement before opening a pull request.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
AEGISS uses uv for the environment and just as the command runner; just with no arguments lists the recipes.

git clone https://github.com/Algorithmiq/AEGISS.git
cd AEGISS
just build --all-groups --all-extras   # every dependency group and the viz extra
uv run prek install                    # git hooks: ruff, ty and the repository checks

In VS Code or GitHub Codespaces, the devcontainer in .devcontainer/ (Ubuntu with uv, just and OpenMPI) runs the two commands above when it starts. The MolTagger GUI needs a display, so it does not run inside the container.

On Nix, nix develop (or direnv with the tracked .envrc) gives a shell with uv, just, lychee and OpenMPI; run the same commands inside it.

docs.title: Day to day
docs.text:
Recipe What it does just fmt format with ruff and apply the safe lint fixes just lint run every git hook on the whole tree, as CI does on a PR just typecheck type-check with ty just test run the test suite (just test -m "not slow" skips the slow tests) just coverage the test suite with branch coverage just docs / just serve-docs build the site strictly / preview it with live reload just doctest run the Python blocks of README.md and docs/ just example run the scripts in examples/ just sbom write CycloneDX SBOMs of the runtime dependencies to sbom/ just sbom-check check them against the license policy in .grant.yaml (needs grant)

The CI workflows call the same recipes, so a red CI job can be reproduced locally by running the recipe it ran.

docs.title: Pull requests
docs.text:
• Branch off main as <type>/<short-description> and target main, bug fixes included; commits to main and to release/* are blocked. Only bots open PRs against release branches.

  • PRs are squash-merged: the PR title and description become the commit on main, and the title becomes the changelog entry, so write it for users. The format is <type>(<optional scope>): <gitmoji> <description>, e.g. fix(projection): 🐛 normalise AO weights, with ! after the type for a breaking change (feat!: 💥 remove the old solver API). The PR checks workflow enforces it.

    Type Use for In the changelog feat new functionality yes fix bug fixes yes deprecate marking something as deprecated yes, with the migration notes perf performance improvements yes docs documentation only yes refactor, test, build, ci, chore, style changes users don't notice no

  • Breaking changes and deprecations need a Migration section in the PR description saying what users have to change, ideally with a before/after example. The PR checks workflow requires it, and it is copied into the changelog.

  • A bug fix that should also reach the current release gets the backport label, before or after merging. Features wait for the next minor release.
  • Fill in the PR template. Changes to the API or to user-facing behaviour come with tests and with the matching documentation update.
  • A new or changed runtime dependency must pass the license policy in .grant.yaml, which the SBOM workflow checks on every PR that touches the dependencies. Record an accepted exception in ignore-packages together with the reason it passes.
  • AEGISS is released under the Apache License 2.0. Every Python file starts with the licence header in .github/license-header.txt; the insert-license git hook adds it to new files.

docs.title: Deprecations
docs.text:
Public functionality is not removed or changed without warning:

  1. Deprecate first. The old behaviour keeps working but emits a DeprecationWarning naming the replacement and the earliest version that removes it; the docstring says the same. The test suite turns warnings into errors, so tests of the deprecated API expect the warning with pytest.warns.
  2. Wait at least one minor release. Something deprecated in 0.5.0 can go in 0.6.0 at the earliest; from 1.0 on, removals only happen in a major release.
  3. Remove. The removal is a breaking change (!) with migration notes.

Names starting with _ and anything documented as experimental can change without a deprecation.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text:
AEGISS follows semantic versioning. Patch releases only fix bugs; before 1.0, a minor release may break existing code, and the changelog lists every breaking change first, with migration notes. Only the newest release is supported.

All work lands on main. Each minor release is stabilised on a release/X.Y branch that only receives backported bug fixes, and a release bot does the tagging and the bookkeeping:

  1. Start. When main is ready, a maintainer checks that no deprecation is due for removal and runs Actions → Release → Run workflow on main (minor, or major for 1.0 and later). The bot creates release/X.Y, tags the first release candidate vX.Y.0rc1 and opens the release PR chore: release vX.Y.0.
  2. Stabilise. Every backported fix merged into release/X.Y before X.Y.0 produces the next release candidate (pip install --pre aegiss==X.Y.0rcN) and updates the release PR.
  3. Release. A maintainer reviews the changelog in the release PR and merges it. The bot tags vX.Y.Z, and the tag runs deploy.yml: it builds the sdist and wheel, checks their version against the tag, creates a draft GitHub release with the files and CycloneDX SBOMs of the runtime dependencies attached, publishes to PyPI through trusted publishing with build-provenance attestations, and publishes the GitHub release, which makes it immutable. The bot then copies CHANGELOG.md back to main. If the release's docs version is missing from the site, run gh workflow run docs.yml --ref vX.Y.Z.
  4. Patch. After X.Y.0, the first backport opens the release PR for X.Y.1; merge it when the fixes should ship. Patch releases have no release candidates.

just changelog previews the next release's entry. CHANGELOG.md is generated by git-cliff from the PR titles and migration notes; fix its wording in the release PR, never by hand on main. It starts at the v0.0.0 tag, which marks where this process was adopted.

The version comes from the git tag (hatch-vcs). Untagged commits on main carry the next minor version (0.3.0.devN while release/0.2 is open), those on release/X.Y the next patch or release candidate.

The documentation site has one version per minor release, the newest of them under latest, and dev for main. docs.yml updates dev on every push to main and the release's version when it is tagged.

A published release never changes: a broken one is yanked on PyPI and replaced by a new patch release. Check a release and its files with gh release verify vX.Y.Z and gh attestation verify <file> --repo Algorithmiq/AEGISS.

docs.title: Dependency updates
docs.text: Dependabot opens weekly grouped updates for the Python dependencies and the GitHub Actions; ruff and ty are bumped monthly by update-tools.yml, together with their prek hooks. block2 is never bumped automatically, since DMRG results depend on its version.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
AEGISS narrows a candidate orbital space with two independent criteria and keeps the orbitals that pass both: the single-orbital entanglement entropy from a DMRG run, and the weight of each molecular orbital on a user-chosen set of atomic orbitals.

flowchart LR
    scf["initial_guess<br/>build_mol, run_scf"] --> loc["localization<br/>(optional)"]
    loc --> dmrg["wavefunction<br/>run_dmrg_subprocess"]
    scf --> dmrg
    dmrg --> soe["active_space.entropy_screening<br/>entropy window"]
    scf --> proj["active_space.ao_projection<br/>AO weights"]
    soe --> sel["active_space.aegiss<br/>select_aegiss"]
    proj --> sel

docs.title: Package layout
docs.text: Module Role aegiss.initial_guess molecule construction and SCF (RHF/UHF/RKS/UKS, solvent, relativistic) aegiss.localization localized orbitals (Boys, Edmiston-Ruedenberg, Pipek-Mezey, IBO, IAO), natural and frozen natural orbitals, all behind the localize dispatcher aegiss.wavefunction DMRG through block2main as a subprocess, and correlated wavefunctions (MP2, CISD, CCSD) aegiss.active_space entropy screening, AO projection, and select_aegiss, which combines them aegiss.config_dataclasses the DMRGConfig, EntropyConfig, ProjectionConfig and OutputConfig inputs, validated on construction aegiss.utils I/O, plotting, environment variables, logging, orbital-index display, MolTagger

docs.title: Conventions that cross modules
docs.text:
• Orbital indices are 0-based internally. User-facing indices honour AEGISS_ORB_BASE (see Orbital Index Base); convert at the boundary with aegiss.utils.orb_display, never in the middle of an algorithm.
  • Unrestricted references run per spin channel. Functions that accept a UHF mean-field return {"alpha": ..., "beta": ...} instead of a single array, and the two channels are never reconciled into one spatial index set (see UHF References).
  • DMRG runs out of process. wavefunction/dmrg_subprocess.py writes an FCIDUMP and a block2main input under SCRATCH_DIR and parses the entropies back, so the block2 Python API is never imported.
  • Configuration is data. New options go into the matching dataclass, with validation in its __post_init__, rather than into new keyword arguments of select_aegiss.

docs.title: Extending
docs.text:
• A new localization method goes in aegiss.localization and is dispatched from localize; add it to the localization tables in the tutorials and in docs/api/localization.md.
  • A new screening criterion follows the shape of entropy_screening and ao_projection: a pure function from orbitals to selected indices, plus a config dataclass, combined in select_aegiss.
  • A new correlated method for natural orbitals goes in wavefunction/methods.py and its dispatcher.

docs.title: Documenting
docs.text:
• Google-style docstrings on every public function and class. The API reference pages under docs/api/ pull them in with mkdocstrings directives such as aegiss.active_space.aegiss.select_aegiss, so a new public symbol needs a directive on the matching page.
  • Python code blocks in docs/ and README.md run as tests (just doctest). A block that cannot run on its own (it needs a DMRG run or a file the reader supplies) is marked notest; a block that continues the previous one is marked continuation. Use the brace form, which Material for MkDocs renders:
```{.python notest}
active = select_aegiss(mol, mf, dmrg_config, entropy_config, projection_config, output_config)
```

In README.md, write python notest instead, so GitHub still highlights the block. - just docs builds with --strict and link and anchor validation. The docs workflow also checks the external links with lychee and deploys the site to the gh-pages branch with mike (just docs-deploy): dev from main, and X.Y (aliased latest) from each release tag. - The tutorial notebooks in docs/tutorials/ are rendered but not executed when the site is built; check them by hand when you change an API they use. - Links inside the notebooks are relative (02_dmrg.ipynb, ../uhf.md), so they work in Jupyter and on GitHub. mkdocs-jupyter does not rewrite them, so they are broken on the site and .lychee.toml skips them until the site is public and they can become absolute site URLs (#91). - The example plots on the Utilities page come from docs/scripts/generate_doc_plots.py (see docs/README.md). - Changes to the public API or to developer workflows update the docs, README.md and AGENTS.md in the same PR.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
AEGISS requires Python ≥ 3.12 and uses uv for dependency management.

git clone https://github.com/Algorithmiq/AEGISS.git
cd AEGISS
uv venv
uv sync
source .venv/bin/activate

docs.title: MolTagger: interactive atom tagging
docs.text:
An interactive 3D molecular viewer for selecting atoms and generating PySCF-compatible ao_labels strings ready to paste into ProjectionConfig. Requires the viz extra:

uv sync --extra viz

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Set these before running any calculation to control memory and scratch space:

Variable Default Description OMP_NUM_THREADS 4 OpenMP threads used by block2 SCRATCH_DIR ./tmp Directory for DMRG scratch files (MPS/MPO) MEM 4 Memory budget in GiB for block2's internal stack PYSCF_MAX_MEMORY 4000 PySCF memory budget in MB AEGISS_ORB_BASE 0 Base (0 or 1) for displaying and interpreting orbital indices — see Orbital index base 
import os
os.environ["OMP_NUM_THREADS"] = "8"
os.environ["SCRATCH_DIR"] = "/scratch/my_job"
os.environ["MEM"] = "32"
os.environ["PYSCF_MAX_MEMORY"] = "16000"

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
AEGISS uses structlog over Python's stdlib logging. Call configure_logging once at the top of your script, before any AEGISS import that triggers logging:

import logging
from aegiss.utils.logging import configure_logging

configure_logging(level=logging.INFO)
# configure_logging(level=logging.DEBUG)  # for per-orbital detail

Output goes to stdout as plain timestamped text. Redirect it to control the destination:

python main.py > log.out         # local — save to file
#SBATCH -o slurm-%j.out          # SLURM — output in slurm-<jobid>.out

configure_logging silences the noisy matplotlib and h5py loggers automatically.

Silence AEGISS selectively (e.g. in a notebook):

logging.getLogger("aegiss").setLevel(logging.WARNING)

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
uv sync --all-groups --all-extras   # install every dependency group (dev, test, docs, …) + extras
prek install                        # install git hooks
pytest                              # run test suite
pytest --cov=aegiss                 # run with coverage report

A bare uv sync installs only the default dev group (ruff, ty, prek, pytest); the test, docs, and interactive groups are opt-in, hence --all-groups above (or, more narrowly, uv sync --group test to just run the suite).

Code style is enforced by ruff (linting + formatting) and ty (type checking). Both run automatically as git hooks (via prek) and in CI.

To build and preview the documentation locally:

uv sync --group docs
mkdocs serve

docs.title: MolTagger
docs.text: Interactive 3D molecular viewer for selecting atoms and generating PySCF-compatible ao_labels strings ready to paste into ProjectionConfig.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
MolTagger requires the viz optional extra:

uv sync --extra viz

This pulls in ase, pyvista, pyvistaqt, qtpy, and PySide6.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
from aegiss.utils.mol_tagger import MolTagger

tagger = MolTagger("my_molecule.xyz")
tagger.show()                 # opens the viewer; blocks until the window is closed
print(tagger.export_tags())   # {atom_index: "Element.N", ...}

docs.title: UI overview
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────┐
│                                             │  Atoms       │
│                                             │  Tag Selected│
│           3D viewport                       │  Atom Info   │
│        (PyVistaQt / VTK)                    │  AO Labels   │
│                                             │  Geometry    │
│                                             │  Export      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────┘

The 3D viewport supports standard mouse navigation: rotate (left-drag), zoom (scroll), pan (middle-drag). Fixed camera orientations are described in the Camera / Navigation section, and aligning the molecule to a plane in Align selection plane.

docs.title: Selecting atoms
docs.text:
Action Effect Right-click atom in 3D view Toggle selection (click, not drag) Click row in Atoms panel Toggle selection from the list Select All / Clear buttons Bulk select / deselect

Selected atoms are highlighted with a translucent red halo in the 3D view and highlighted in the atom list simultaneously. Both views stay in sync.

docs.title: Tagging atoms
docs.text:
1. Select one or more atoms.
  2. Type a whole-number label in the Tag Selected text box (e.g. 0).
  3. Press Apply Tag or Return.

Each tagged atom is stored as Element.N (e.g. C.1, Ru.2). Tags appear next to the atom coordinates in the Atoms list. Remove Tags clears tags from the current selection.

docs.title: Atom Info panel
docs.text: Shows the minimal-basis shell structure for each selected atom:

docs.title: AO Labels panel
docs.text:
Automatically suggests PySCF-compatible ao_labels strings based on the selected atoms and the chosen character mode. The output is ready to copy directly into ProjectionConfig. For example:

["Ru 4d", "N 2pz", "C 2pz"]

Press Copy to send the string to the system clipboard.

docs.title: Character modes
docs.text: Mode Intended use Logic π / Auto π systems, MLCT/LMCT states Metals → d/f shell. Organic atoms → np{axis} where {axis} is the plane-normal detected by SVD planarity analysis. Falls back to all np if non-planar. d-shell Pure metal-centred active spaces Returns only d/f-shell labels for transition metals. Warns if ligand atoms are also selected. σ framework Sigma bonding / lone pair character Organic atoms → ns + the two in-plane np components (complement of the π axis). Custom Manual entry Unlocks the text box for free-form input.

docs.title: Planarity detection
docs.text:
The normal to the molecular plane is found by SVD of the centred position matrix. The planarity score is s₂ / s₁ from the singular values.

Score Verdict Labels emitted < 0.25 Planar C 2pz (or px/py as appropriate) ≥ 0.25 Non-planar All C 2p (warning shown in orange)

docs.title: Align selection plane
docs.text:
The Geometry panel's Align Selection Plane → XY button rotates the whole molecule (about its centroid) so that the best-fit plane of the selected atoms becomes the XY plane, with its normal along Z. It moves the atoms, not the camera, so the 2pz labels then refer to the out-of-plane direction of the selection. It needs at least three non-collinear selected atoms; Ctrl+Z undoes the last alignment.

The alignment is most meaningful for planar selections (score < 0.25); for a non-planar selection the fitted plane is a compromise.

docs.title: Transition metal classification
docs.text:
Range Shell Sc–Zn (Z 21–30) 3d Y–Cd (Z 39–48) 4d La (Z 57), Hf–Hg (Z 72–80) 5d Ce–Lu (Z 58–71) 4f + 5d Ac (Z 89), Rf–Cn (Z 104–112) 6d Th–Lr (Z 90–103) 5f + 6d

Lanthanides and actinides produce two labels because CASSCF active spaces for f-element complexes routinely require both the f and d shells.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Select Ru only → ["Ru 4d"]

Select Ru + bpy C/N atoms in π / Auto mode: 

["Ru 4d", "C 2pz", "N 2pz"]   # assuming z is the ring-plane normal

Select Ce in d-shell mode: 

["Ce 4f", "Ce 5d"]

docs.title: Mouse controls
docs.text: Action Effect Left-click + drag Rotate Scroll wheel Zoom in / out Middle-click + drag Pan Right-click Select atom (does not move camera)

docs.title: Fixed orientations
docs.text:
Six preset buttons snap the camera to a standard plane-aligned view, keeping the current molecule centre:

Button Plane shown XY XY plane (top view) XZ XZ plane (front view) YZ YZ plane (side view) XY*, XZ*, YZ* The same planes, seen from the opposite side

docs.title: Tagged XYZ format
docs.text:
Save Tagged XYZ writes a standard XYZ file where tagged atoms use the Element.N label instead of the bare element symbol:

12

C.1     -1.212345   0.000000   0.000000
C.1      1.212345   0.000000   0.000000
N.2     -2.345678   1.000000   0.000000
Ru.3     0.000000   0.000000   0.000000
H        1.500000   1.000000   0.000000

The file can be reloaded into MolTagger; tags are automatically recovered from the Element.N labels.

docs.title: Orbital index base
docs.text:
AEGISS stores and computes every orbital index 0-based — the PySCF convention. Many quantum-chemistry users, however, prefer to read and type orbital indices 1-based (the Fortran convention used by ORCA, Molpro, Molcas, …). AEGISS lets you choose that base for display and input without ever changing what happens internally.

The base affects only:

  • how indices are printed — logs, plot labels, cube-file names; and
  • how indices you pass in are interpreted before being converted back to the internal 0-based representation.

It never affects stored values, array slicing, or the indices returned by the API — those are always 0-based, so results round-trip safely regardless of the setting.

docs.title: Choosing the base
docs.text:
Set it once after installation with the aegiss CLI:

aegiss config set-base 1      # print/read orbital indices 1-based (ORCA/Molpro style)
aegiss config set-base 0      # back to the 0-based default
aegiss config get-base        # show the currently resolved base
aegiss config path            # show the config-file location

The choice is persisted to ${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-~/.config}/aegiss/config.toml.

docs.title: Resolution precedence
docs.text:
The base is resolved on first use (then cached for the process) in this order:

Priority Source Notes 1 (highest) AEGISS_ORB_BASE environment variable Per-run override; wins over the file 2 orbital_base in the config file Written by aegiss config set-base 3 Default 0 
# Force 0-based for a single run, even if config.toml says orbital_base = 1:
AEGISS_ORB_BASE=0 python your_script.py

Set it before the pipeline runs

orbital_base() is resolved lazily on the first index that is printed or interpreted, then cached. Set AEGISS_ORB_BASE (or the shell prefix) before calling any AEGISS selection function. If you change it mid-process — e.g. in a notebook — call aegiss.utils.orb_display.reset_cache() afterwards.

docs.title: The input/output contract
docs.text:
Inputs use the configured base, but return values are always 0-based

This asymmetry is deliberate — it keeps returned indices safe to slice mo_coeff[:, idx], save to disk, and feed back into the pipeline regardless of the base.

With AEGISS_ORB_BASE=1:

from aegiss.active_space.ao_projection import select_by_ao_projection

# You pass 1-based indices …
selected = select_by_ao_projection(
    mf, ao_labels=["C 2pz"], restricted_space=[35, 36, 37]
)
# … but `selected` comes back 0-based:
#   array([34, 35, 36])

Passing indices. Give them in your configured base. Affected parameters:

Function Parameter select_by_ao_projection restricted_space (a plain list[int] only) mo_ao_contributions mo_indices localize_fnos active, frozen

An index below the base — e.g. 0 when the base is 1 — raises ValueError rather than silently producing a negative index:

>>> select_by_ao_projection(mf, ao_labels=["C 2pz"], restricted_space=[0, 1])
ValueError: Orbital indices [0] are invalid for base 1 (expected >= 1).

Don't re-feed returned indices as base-1 input

Because results are 0-based, passing a returned array straight back in as a plain index list while in base 1 would shift it down a second time ([34, 35, 36] → [33, 34, 35]). Returned indices are the canonical 0-based form meant for slicing and saving — not for re-typing as user input. To display them in your base, wrap them:

from aegiss.utils.orb_display import to_display_all
to_display_all(selected)   # [35, 36, 37] under base 1

docs.title: What stays 0-based
docs.text:
Only a plain list of integers is treated as base-dependent user input. Values produced by AEGISS internals are always 0-based and are never re-shifted:

  • (index, entropy) pair-lists and (occ_list, virt_list) tuples from select_by_entropy (as passed through restricted_space);
  • every value returned by the public API (select_by_ao_projection, select_aegiss, mo_ao_contributions dict keys, get_subspaces_from_cas, …).

This is why a full select_aegiss run is unaffected internally: it hands the pair/tuple forms between stages, so no double-shift can occur even under AEGISS_ORB_BASE=1 — the only visible change is the base shown in the logs.

docs.title: Programmatic access
docs.text:
The resolver and converters live in aegiss.utils.orb_display:

from aegiss.utils.orb_display import (
    orbital_base,     # -> 0 or 1, the resolved base
    to_display,       # 0-based int      -> display base
    to_display_all,   # 0-based iterable -> display base (list)
    from_display,     # display-base int      -> 0-based (raises below base)
    from_display_all, # display-base iterable -> 0-based (raises below base)
    reset_cache,      # clear the cached base after changing env/config
)

docs.title: Choosing parameters
docs.text:
How the AEGISS authors choose the DMRG window, the screening and projection thresholds and the atomic-orbital labels. The AEGISS agent skill follows the same rules: it ships the text below.

Rules from the AEGISS authors (preprint and an interview). Where the authors have no tested recipe the text says so: a selection made there is exploratory and the user must be told. Pass every threshold explicitly, and do not carry a threshold from one system to another: thresholds are not transferable.

docs.title: Reference and orbitals
docs.text: Situation Rule Why Closed-shell molecule Start from canonical RHF orbitals. The DMRG window is an index window around the Fermi level, so it needs energy-ordered orbitals. Open-shell molecule Use UHF. ROHF is untested in AEGISS; use UHF for open shells. AEGISS offers only UHF for open shells. UHF reference Check ⟨S²⟩ before the DMRG: the deviation from S(S+1) must be at most 10% of S(S+1). Beyond that, flag it to the user instead of continuing silently. Spin contamination of the UHF orbitals carries into the entropies. Spin-summed or spin-resolved entropies Follow the guidance on UHF references. Spin-resolved needs symm_type="SZ". The criteria are on that page. Many low-lying virtuals of little importance (Rydberg-like or diffuse functions in a large basis) Start from natural orbitals (NOs). Canonical virtuals with little correlation sit just above the LUMO and fill the window; NOs carry almost no occupation there and move them down the list. Canonical window would approach about 100 orbitals Use NOs together with reorder="fiedler", with a smaller window. NOs concentrate the correlation in fewer orbitals, so a smaller window covers the same physics and the DMRG is cheaper. Canonical RHF is known beforehand to be a poor reference Use NOs from a correlated method (the paper uses MP2). They adapt better to the correlation than canonical RHF orbitals. Localized orbitals Do not use them as input. They have no orbital energies, so the index window is no longer a Fermi-level window, and there is no workaround yet. Cheap steps in a smaller basis Do it only if the basis is much smaller; the saving is otherwise small. Redo the final selection in the production basis. The DMRG dominates the cost and its cost is set by the window size. The setup (labels, thresholds) carries over, but orbital indices change with the basis, so the final selection does not.

docs.title: DMRG window
docs.text: Situation Rule Why Starting ncas Start with 3m, where m is the expected number of active orbitals. General guideline of the authors. Organic π systems Expect to need 3–5m. Range found for the systems of the paper. Transition-metal complexes Expect to need 6–8m. The d manifold is spread in energy and mixes with ligand orbitals. Bond breaking No tested factor; start with 3m and treat the result as exploratory. The authors have no example. Margin to the edge Keep at least 3 orbitals between the outermost orbital above τ_E and each edge of the window. A crowded edge means correlated orbitals may lie outside the window. Margin smaller than 3 Widen the window by about 5 orbitals on the crowded side and rerun the DMRG. The entropy ranking is only meaningful for orbitals well inside the window. Closed-shell RHF symm_type="SU2". Cheaper at equal accuracy. UHF, spin-resolved entropies, or any open-shell case with per-spin data symm_type="SZ" (the library default). UHF and spin-resolved entropies require it. Large window, or poor convergence at a given bond dimension Use reorder="fiedler". Authors' guideline: reordering shortens the interaction range along the DMRG chain, which helps large windows converge.

docs.title: Bond dimension
docs.text: Run max_bond_dim Why Cheap first look 200. Trust the set of orbitals above τ_E only if a rerun at 500 gives the same set; If 500 is not converged, check at 800/1000 (based on the DMRG expected cost); With a ncas >= 50 the suggestion is to run the exploratory run at 500 and check with 800/1000 The ranking can be unreliable at low bond dimension; an unchanged set at 500 shows it has converged. Production 500, a multiple of 4. The library ramps from max_bond_dim/2; the paper ramps from 100 to 500 (Trans-Cl: fixed 500). Value used by every run of the paper. Checking convergence Rerun at a higher max_bond_dim and stop when the set above τ_E is unchanged. The library runs the whole ramp in one DMRG call and computes the entropies only from the final wavefunction, so there are no entropies partway through the ramp.

docs.title: Entropy screening
docs.text: Situation Rule Why Starting point fraction=0.1, fraction_type="r" (τ_E = S(1)max/10). The paper uses 0.2 for benzene. The AutoCAS criterion, used by the paper. Flat entropies (every orbital above the 0.1 threshold) Raise to fraction=0.9, relative. In the paper's DOBNA case with MP2 natural orbitals no orbital fell below 0.1; 0.9 isolated the strongly entropic subset. Comparing entropies across runs fraction_type="a". An absolute threshold is the same number in every run; a relative one moves with S(1)max. S(1)max itself is small fraction_type="a". A relative cut then keeps orbitals that are only weakly correlated. Occupied and virtual entropies differ strongly in scale ranking="subset". A global cut would empty one side. Any run Pass fraction, fraction_type and ranking explicitly. The defaults differ between the config classes and the selection functions, and are being aligned (open PRs #112 and #114).

docs.title: Atom labelling
docs.text: Situation Rule Why Localized process (d–d, π→π*, bond dissociation) Use 2–3 clusters and put labels only on the active cluster. In ferrocene only "Fe 3d" is labelled; the Cp orbitals enter through the entropy step. Select the cluster's atoms in MolTagger to get atom-specific ao_labels. The entropy step brings in the correlated partners; the labels only say which process matters. Delocalized or charge-transfer process Put donor and acceptor in separate clusters (Trans-Cl: Ru and the ligand). Each channel then gets its own threshold or top_n. Extended ligand One cluster per ring or fragment (TLD-1433). Each ring or fragment then gets its own threshold or top_n (TLD-1433 uses 4 clusters). Cannot anticipate where the relevant orbitals are localised Skip clustering: the labels apply to every atom of that element (the AVAS-like limit). Without clusters the labels are not tied to a region of the molecule. Refining the labels Go from coarse to fine and refine only when the selection is unbalanced. Relabelling does not need a new DMRG run, only the AO projection step. The DMRG is the expensive part and does not depend on the labels. Choosing the molecular plane for 2pz labels Orient the molecule so the π orbitals are along z, or use the matching label (2px if the molecule lies in the yz plane, as DOBNA does). Use MolTagger to check. MolTagger can be used to identify the plane in which the selected atoms are placed. A label on the wrong p orbital selects nothing useful. Bad clustering Expect a less compact space, not a lost orbital. Clustering never removes correlated orbitals from the entropy-screened pool.

docs.title: AO projection
docs.text: Situation Rule Why Clean, well-separated target manifold (benzene π, ferrocene Fe 3d, DOBNA π) contribution=0.5 with contribution_type="a". The weights separate cleanly, so a threshold picks the manifold. Strongly mixed orbitals (metal–ligand hybridization, Rydberg virtuals) top_n instead of contribution. Trans-Cl: top_n=1 per Ru 4d component and (4,4) occupied/virtual on the bipyridine π (space II: 2 per component and (6,6)); TLD-1433 uses top_n per cluster. A threshold takes either everything or nothing there. Balance between occupied and virtual orbitals top_n with ranking="subset" (ProjectionConfig only). This gives the (n_occ, n_virt) count. Reading the weights Do not treat a contribution value as a probability. The weight sums the absolute AO–MO overlaps over the label's AOs (an L1 norm of non-orthogonal overlaps), so it is not bounded by 1 (open issue, PR #10). Distinct correlation channels (metal and ligand) One group per channel, each with its own threshold or top_n. Each channel then gets its own selection. One manifold described by several labels (["C 2pz", "N 2pz"] for one π system) A flat list or a single group. One threshold fits one manifold. 4d/5d metal without a pseudopotential Do not run with basis="minao". Without a pseudopotential minao mis-numbers the 4d/5d labels and the selection comes out empty; open PR #113 makes it raise. Label outside the minimal valence shell (a second d shell, Rydberg or diffuse functions) ProjectionConfig(basis=None) (projected_basis=None in select_by_ao_projection). The minimal basis has no such functions. Any run Pass contribution, contribution_type, top_n and, in ProjectionConfig, ranking explicitly. The defaults differ between the config classes and the selection functions (open PRs #112 and #114).

docs.title: Typical AO labels
docs.text: System ao_labels Notes Conjugated π "C 2pz", plus the heteroatoms ("N 2pz", "B 2pz", "O 2pz") 2pz assumes the molecule lies in the xy plane; the paper writes C/B 2px for DOBNA, which lies in the yz plane. 3d metal "Fe 3d" 4d metal "Ru 4d", or the five d components separately with top_n=1 each Needs a pseudopotential, see above. Ligand of a metal Its own group, e.g. ["C 2pz", "N 2pz"] on the ligand atoms The paper writes this as C/N 2pz. Bond breaking (σ/σ*) No tested recipe Not analysed by the authors; the selection is exploratory. Lone pairs No tested recipe Not analysed by the authors; the selection is exploratory. Main-group radical No tested recipe Not analysed by the authors; the selection is exploratory. 4s, or a second d shell (3d′) on a metal No tested recipe Not analysed by the authors; the selection is exploratory.

docs.title: Stability check
docs.text: Rerun the fraction_type=r selection with fraction 0.08, 0.10 and 0.12. The final active space should be identical; the entropy-screened pool may shift by an orbital or two, because the AO projection absorbs that. If the final space changes, an orbital sits right at the threshold: inspect it (cube file, AO composition) and look for a plateau in the threshold plot, AutoCAS style. The paper does not test this check.

docs.title: Hand-off limit
docs.text:
You may run DMRG yourself (as an agent) unless both ncas ≥ 30 and max_bond_dim ≥ 500; then hand the user a script. A cheap, low-bond-dimension run is fine on any window. For reference, block2 defaults on one node:

System CAS max_bond_dim Threads DMRG time Ferrocene (40,40) 300 32 (LEONARDO) 654 s (about 11 min) DOBNA (40,40) 300 32 (LEONARDO) 291 s (about 5 min)

docs.title: Final checks
docs.text:
Check the final active space against this list; each line gives the check and what is a red flag.

  • Electron count: an odd count for a closed shell, or a count that does not match the chemistry.
  • Occupied/virtual pairs: an occupied orbital whose correlating partner is missing, or an almost all-virtual space.
  • Degenerate partners: one orbital of a degenerate pair selected without the other (top_n can split a pair; use it carefully).
  • Frontier orbitals: HOMO or LUMO missing.
  • Rydberg-like or diffuse virtuals: a virtual with a diffuse shape, or a low total weight on the minimal-basis AOs. Remove it by hand (the paper does so for TLD-1433).
  • Window edge: high entropy near the edge of the window; widen the window.
  • Occupations after CASSCF: natural occupation numbers above 1.98 or below 0.02 (generic thresholds).
  • UHF: an unequal number of alpha and beta orbitals.
  • Symmetry: optionally compare irreducible representations (the paper uses them as a post-selection criterion).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Choosing the wrong plane for the 2pz labels. MolTagger helps.
  • Labelling a 4d/5d metal without a pseudopotential.
  • Using too small a window.
  • Carrying thresholds from one system to another: they are not transferable.
  • Index base confusion: inputs follow AEGISS_ORB_BASE, but the returned indices are always 0-based; see Orbital index base.
  • Accepting the output without looking at the orbitals.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
just test                  # the whole suite
just test -m "not slow"    # skip the tests that take a minute or more
just coverage              # branch coverage, written to coverage.xml
just doctest               # the Python blocks of README.md and docs/
just example               # the scripts in examples/
  • Tests live in tests/, one test_<module>.py per source module; the name-tests-test hook enforces the naming.
  • Quantum-chemistry tests use small molecules and minimal basis sets. Mock block2/DMRG unless the test is about DMRG, and mark anything that runs for a minute or more with @pytest.mark.slow.
  • Warnings are errors (filterwarnings = ["error"] in pyproject.toml). Fix the cause; when a warning comes from a dependency, add a targeted ignore entry with a comment saying why.
  • CI runs the suite on Linux x86_64, Linux aarch64 and macOS arm64 with Python 3.12 and 3.14, the platforms block2 publishes wheels for.

docs.title: Unrestricted (UHF) references
docs.text:
AEGISS supports unrestricted (UHF) mean-fields end to end. Because the alpha and beta molecular orbitals of a UHF reference are different sets of functions, the pipeline runs per spin channel from the DMRG single-orbital entropies all the way to the final orbital indices, and returns the alpha and beta selections separately — they are never reconciled into one spatial index set.

This page describes how the three regimes (restricted, UHF spin-summed, UHF spin-resolved) differ, how to configure them, and how the spin-summed and spin-resolved single-orbital entropies (SOE) compare.

docs.title: Workflow at a glance
docs.text:
The same four stages run in every regime; what is shared versus split between the spin channels is the only thing that changes.

Stage RHF UHF — summed UHF — resolved DMRG SOE (run_dmrg_subprocess) one 1-D list one 1-D list (spin-summed) one (2, ncas) array — α and β rows Entropy screen select_by_entropy → 1 window select_by_entropy → 1 window select_by_spin_entropy → 2 windows MO coefficients one (nao, nmo) matrix two blocks mo_coeff[0/1] two blocks mo_coeff[0/1] AO contributions one pass two passes, shared window two passes, own window each Result spatial ndarray {"alpha", "beta"} {"alpha", "beta"}

The only difference between summed and resolved is the search space

From the MO-coefficient split onward, UHF-summed and UHF-resolved are identical: two coefficient blocks → two AO-contribution lists → a split alpha/beta selection. They differ only in the entropy screening step — resolved gives each channel its own window, summed shares the single spin-summed window across both channels.

A restricted mf (2-D mo_coeff) always takes the RHF column regardless of configuration: there is only one coefficient set to project.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Three DMRGConfig fields control the UHF behaviour:

from aegiss.config_dataclasses import DMRGConfig

dmrg_config = DMRGConfig(
    ncas=20,
    nelecas=(11, 9),      # (nalpha, nbeta); nalpha - nbeta must equal mol.spin
    symm_type="SZ",       # required for UHF and for spin-resolved SOE
    unrestricted=None,    # None → autodetect isinstance(mf, scf.uhf.UHF)
    spin_soe="auto",      # "auto" | "summed" | "resolved"
)
  • unrestricted — whether to emit an unrestricted (IUHF=1) FCIDUMP with separate aa/bb/ab integral blocks. None (default) autodetects from the mean-field type; pass True/False to override. UHF requires symm_type="SZ".
  • symm_type — must be "SZ" for UHF (the spin-adapted "SU2" path cannot represent an unrestricted state), and also for spin-resolved SOE (the per-spin 1-PDM is only available without spin adaptation).

  • spin_soe — selects spin-summed or spin-resolved single-orbital entropies. The resolution rule (DMRGConfig.spin_resolved()):

    spin_soe Result "resolved" spin-resolved (requires symm_type="SZ") "summed" spin-summed "auto" resolved iff nalpha != nbeta and symm_type="SZ", else summed

Reference spin must match the active spin

For a UHF reference a single active-orbital window only exists when the frozen cores of the two spin channels coincide, i.e. the reference spin polarisation equals the requested active spin: \(N_\alpha^{\text{ref}} - N_\beta^{\text{ref}} = n_\alpha - n_\beta\). get_subspaces_from_cas raises a ValueError otherwise.

docs.title: Spin-summed vs. spin-resolved SOE
docs.text: The single-orbital entropy quantifies how entangled an orbital is with the rest of the active space. What "an orbital" means differs between the two flavours.

docs.title: Spin-summed (4-state spatial orbital)
docs.text:
Each spatial orbital is treated as a four-state subsystem — empty, alpha-only, beta-only, doubly occupied — so its entropy is

\[ S_i = -\sum_{\mu \in \{d,\, \alpha,\, \beta,\, 0\}} \omega_\mu \ln \omega_\mu, \qquad \omega = \bigl\{\, d_i,\; n_i^\alpha - d_i,\; n_i^\beta - d_i,\; 1 - n_i + d_i \,\bigr\}, \]

where \(n_i = n_i^\alpha + n_i^\beta\) is the spatial occupation and \(d_i\) the double occupation (recovered from the 1-PDM and 1-NPC diagonals). This yields a single ranking and, downstream, a single spatial active-space window.

docs.title: Spin-resolved (2-state spin-orbital)
docs.text:
Each spin-orbital is a two-state mode (occupied / empty), so its entropy is the binary entropy of the spin-orbital occupation \(n_i^\sigma = \text{PDM}_\sigma[i,i]\):

\[ H(n_i^\sigma) = -\,n_i^\sigma \ln n_i^\sigma - (1 - n_i^\sigma)\ln(1 - n_i^\sigma), \qquad \sigma \in \{\alpha, \beta\}. \]

The alpha and beta channels are then thresholded independently, so the two active windows can contain different orbitals — precisely the spin-polarised situation where an orbital carries a fractional occupation (and hence correlation) that differs between the two channels, e.g. \(n_i^\alpha \approx 0.9\) while \(n_i^\beta \approx 0.1\). (A cleanly singly-occupied orbital, \(n_i^\alpha = 1,\ n_i^\beta = 0\), is a product state with \(H = 0\) in both channels — and \(S_i = 0\) spatially too — so it is not, and should not be, flagged by either measure.)

What spin-resolved SOE keeps and drops

\(H(n_i^\alpha)\) and \(H(n_i^\beta)\) are the two marginals of the joint two-mode (spatial-orbital) state whose entropy is the spin-summed \(S_i\). By subadditivity \(S_i \le S_i^\alpha + S_i^\beta\), with equality only when the two spin modes of the orbital are uncorrelated. So spin-resolved SOE exposes the per-channel asymmetry that spin-summed averages over, but at the cost of discarding the intra-orbital \(\alpha\)–\(\beta\) correlation (the double-occupancy fluctuation \(d_i \neq n_i^\alpha n_i^\beta\)). For static correlation localised within a single spatial orbital, the spin-summed \(S_i\) is the more faithful single number.

docs.title: Which to use
docs.text:
• Spin-summed — closed-shell-like or weakly polarised targets, or whenever both channels should be screened on one shared entropy window. This is the "auto" choice when \(n_\alpha = n_\beta\).
  • Spin-resolved — strongly spin-polarised / open-shell targets where the alpha and beta correlation patterns genuinely differ. This is the "auto" choice when \(n_\alpha \neq n_\beta\) (and symm_type="SZ").

docs.title: Degenerate targets
docs.text:
The entropies are computed in the fixed reference \(S_z\) sector — the SZ DMRG targets spin = nalpha - nbeta. This is well-defined and reproducible, but for a spin-degenerate open-shell target (a term with \(S > 0\) has an \(M_s = -S, \dots, +S\) manifold) the entropies are those of the specific \(M_s\) component that nalpha - nbeta selects:

  • This affects the spin-summed path too — it is the same SZ run — so it is not introduced by spin resolution.
  • At the extremal \(M_s\), the majority-spin closed / singly-occupied orbitals have integer occupation, so \(H(n^\sigma) = 0\) there; the per-channel split reflects that sector's attribution (one channel can be frozen).
  • The alpha and beta selections are therefore specific to that \(M_s\) sector. They are not merged into a union: index \(k\) is a different MO in each channel, so the two lists stay independent (see The UHF active space).

A spatially degenerate target (a bare atom — e.g. the \(^3P\) ground state of oxygen is also orbitally three-fold degenerate) lets DMRG pick an arbitrary component of the spatial manifold; this is a general active-space-selection caveat, unrelated to spin resolution. Molecular targets with a non-degenerate reference avoid it.

docs.title: AO projection on a UHF reference
docs.text:
select_by_ao_projection detects a UHF reference from a 3-D mf.mo_coeff of shape (2, nao, nmo) and screens each spin block separately. The AO overlaps (\(\langle \text{minao}_\mu | \text{AO}_\nu \rangle\) via intor_cross) are spin-independent, so only the MO coefficients differ between channels.

from aegiss.active_space import select_by_ao_projection

result = select_by_ao_projection(
    mf,                       # UHF: mo_coeff.ndim == 3
    ao_labels=["C 2pz"],
    contribution=0.5,
    contribution_type="a",
)
# result == {"alpha": np.ndarray, "beta": np.ndarray}

The restricted_space argument decides whether the channels share a window:

  • a plain list / (occ, virt) tuple → shared by both channels (spin-summed);
  • a {"alpha": ..., "beta": ...} dict (as produced by select_by_spin_entropy) → each channel is restricted to its own window (spin-resolved).

Passing a spin-resolved dict together with a restricted mf raises a ValueError.

The contribution threshold follows the same pattern: a float or per-label list is shared by both channels, while a {"alpha": ..., "beta": ...} dict applies a different threshold to each spin channel (each value may itself be a float or per-label list). This is orthogonal to restricted_space — you can share the window but cut the channels at different weights:

result = select_by_ao_projection(
    mf,                       # UHF: mo_coeff.ndim == 3
    ao_labels=["C 2pz"],
    contribution={"alpha": 0.2, "beta": 0.5},   # stricter cut on beta
    contribution_type="r",
)

As with a spin-resolved restricted_space, passing a contribution dict together with a restricted mf raises a ValueError.

docs.title: Full pipeline
docs.text:
select_aegiss wires everything together. Its return type reflects the reference: a single np.ndarray for a restricted mean-field, or a split {"alpha": ..., "beta": ...} mapping for a UHF one.

from aegiss.initial_guess import build_mol, run_scf
from aegiss.active_space import select_aegiss
from aegiss.config_dataclasses import (
    DMRGConfig, EntropyConfig, ProjectionConfig, OutputConfig,
)

mol = build_mol("open_shell.xyz", basis="ccpvdz", spin=2)  # triplet: matches nelecas=(11, 9)
mf  = run_scf(mol, method="UHF")

active = select_aegiss(
    mol, mf,
    dmrg_config=DMRGConfig(ncas=20, nelecas=(11, 9), symm_type="SZ", spin_soe="resolved"),
    entropy_config=EntropyConfig(fraction=0.1, fraction_type="r", ranking="global"),
    projection_config=ProjectionConfig(ao_labels=["C 2pz"], contribution=0.5),
    output_config=OutputConfig(saving_folder="./orbs/"),
)
# active == {"alpha": np.ndarray, "beta": np.ndarray}

The alpha and beta selections are not reconciled

Index \(k\) refers to a different MO in each spin channel, so there is no common spatial active space to merge them into — the split is kept deliberately. When output is enabled, cube files and any per-channel plots are written with _alpha / _beta tags; the AO pie-contribution plot (which expects a single flat orbital list) is skipped for the split selection.

docs.title: The UHF active space
docs.text:
For a UHF reference the active space is two independent lists of MO indices, one per spin channel: active["alpha"] indexes the columns of mf.mo_coeff[0] and active["beta"] those of mf.mo_coeff[1]. The two lists are never merged into a union or an intersection, since the same index denotes different orbitals in the two channels.

The lists must satisfy one condition: the same number of alpha and beta orbitals. An unrestricted CAS has a single number of active orbitals, ncas, shared by both channels. AEGISS selects each channel independently and does not enforce this, so check the two lengths and adjust the selection before building the CAS.

The active electrons of each channel are the occupied orbitals in its list; the remaining occupied orbitals of that channel are its core. With equal lengths, the two lists define an unrestricted CAS in PySCF (indices are 0-based, hence base=0):

from pyscf import mcscf

alpha, beta = active["alpha"], active["beta"]
assert len(alpha) == len(beta), "an unrestricted CAS needs as many alpha as beta orbitals"

nelecas = (int(mf.mo_occ[0][alpha].sum()), int(mf.mo_occ[1][beta].sum()))
mc = mcscf.UCASCI(mf, len(alpha), nelecas)
mo = mc.sort_mo((list(alpha), list(beta)), base=0)
mc.kernel(mo)
print(mc.fcisolver.spin_square(mc.ci, mc.ncas, mc.nelecas))  # (<S^2>, 2S+1)

Two consequences of different alpha and beta spaces:

  • The CAS wavefunction is in general not an eigenfunction of \(S^2\); check \(\langle S^2 \rangle\) of the solution, as in the last line above.
  • The CAS needs unrestricted solvers: UCASCI / UCASSCF in PySCF, or an unrestricted (IUHF=1) FCIDUMP for DMRG. PySCF's NEVPT2 does not accept an unrestricted CAS.

docs.title: Validating the entropies against an exact reference
docs.text:
Both AEGISS entropy reconstructions are exact only because the reduced density matrices are diagonal under particle-number symmetry:

  • _compute_soe builds the 4-state spatial \(S_i\) from the 1-PDM + 1-NPC diagonals;
  • _compute_spin_soe builds the 2-state per-spin \(H(n_i^\sigma)\) from the 1-PDM diagonal.

Both can be checked against the definition directly. For a system small enough for full CI, the state is a list of determinants with weights \(|c_{\alpha\beta}|^2\), and the single-orbital reduced density matrix of orbital \(i\) is diagonal in its four local states (empty, \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), double). Its eigenvalues are therefore just the summed weights of the determinants in which orbital \(i\) is in each state, and summing over one spin gives the per-spin occupations. The check below computes the entropies this way from the CI coefficients, with no density-matrix code, and compares them with what AEGISS's functions return from PySCF's RDMs.

The reference must be non-degenerate (see Degenerate targets). A stretched-H₂ broken-symmetry singlet fits: \(S = 0\) is non-degenerate, yet the UHF orbitals are genuinely spin-polarised (\(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) localise on opposite atoms). It is reached by following the RHF→UHF instability — no arbitrary density seeding. With two orbitals and two electrons, PySCF's FCI is exact, so there is nothing to converge.

import numpy as np
from pyscf import ao2mo, fci, gto, scf
from pyscf.fci import cistring

from aegiss.wavefunction.dmrg_subprocess import _compute_soe, _compute_spin_soe

# Stretched H2/STO-3G: a closed-shell singlet with a broken-symmetry UHF
# solution, reached by following the RHF->UHF instability.
mol = gto.M(atom="H 0 0 0; H 0 0 2.5", basis="sto-3g", spin=0, verbose=0)
mf = scf.UHF(mol).run()
for _ in range(2):
    mo = mf.stability()[0]
    if np.allclose(mo, mf.mo_coeff):
        break
    mf = mf.run(mf.make_rdm1(mo, mf.mo_occ))

# FCI in the UHF orbitals (alpha and beta orbitals differ, as in AEGISS's UHF DMRG)
ca, cb = mf.mo_coeff
n, nelec = ca.shape[1], mol.nelec
h1 = (ca.T @ mf.get_hcore() @ ca, cb.T @ mf.get_hcore() @ cb)
eri = (ao2mo.full(mol, ca), ao2mo.general(mol, (ca, ca, cb, cb)), ao2mo.full(mol, cb))
solver = fci.direct_uhf.FCISolver(mol)
e_fci, civec = solver.kernel(h1, eri, n, nelec, ecore=mol.energy_nuc())

# --- AEGISS: entropies from the RDMs, as the DMRG path computes them ---
(dm1a, dm1b), (_, dm2ab, _) = solver.make_rdm12s(civec, n, nelec)
pdm1 = np.array([dm1a, dm1b])                                     # (2, n, n)
dbl = np.array([dm2ab[i, i, i, i] for i in range(n)])             # <n_ia n_ib> (double occ.)
npc1 = np.zeros_like(pdm1)
npc1[0] = np.diag(dm1a.diagonal() + dm1b.diagonal() + 2 * dbl)    # 1-NPC diagonal <N_i^2>
s_spatial = _compute_soe(pdm1, npc1)                              # spin-summed path
Ha, Hb = _compute_spin_soe(pdm1)                                  # spin-resolved path

# --- Reference: the definition, straight from the CI coefficients ---
def entropy(p):
    return -sum(x * np.log(x) for x in p if x > 1e-14)

alpha = cistring.make_strings(range(n), nelec[0])                 # occupation bit strings
beta = cistring.make_strings(range(n), nelec[1])
weight = np.abs(civec) ** 2                                       # weight[alpha, beta]
s_ref, h_ref = np.zeros(n), np.zeros((2, n))
for i in range(n):
    p = np.zeros((2, 2))                                          # p[occ_alpha, occ_beta] of orbital i
    for ia, a in enumerate(alpha):
        for ib, b in enumerate(beta):
            p[(a >> i) & 1, (b >> i) & 1] += weight[ia, ib]
    s_ref[i] = entropy(p.ravel())                                 # 4-state spatial S(1)
    h_ref[:, i] = entropy(p.sum(axis=1)), entropy(p.sum(axis=0))  # per-spin S(1)

assert np.allclose(s_spatial, s_ref, atol=1e-10)
assert np.allclose([Ha, Hb], h_ref, atol=1e-10)

np.set_printoptions(precision=4, suppress=True, floatmode="fixed")
print("spatial S(1)  reference     :", s_ref)
print("              _compute_soe  :", s_spatial)
print("per-spin a/b  reference     :", h_ref[0], h_ref[1])
print("        _compute_spin_soe   :", Ha, Hb)
print("subadditivity |Ha-Hb| <= S_spatial <= Ha+Hb:",
      np.abs(Ha - Hb), "<=", s_spatial, "<=", Ha + Hb)

Output:

spatial S(1)  reference     : [0.7439 0.7439]
              _compute_soe  : [0.7439 0.7439]
per-spin a/b  reference     : [0.6930 0.6930] [0.6930 0.6930]
        _compute_spin_soe   : [0.6930 0.6930] [0.6930 0.6930]
subadditivity |Ha-Hb| <= S_spatial <= Ha+Hb: [0.0000 0.0000] <= [0.7439 0.7439] <= [1.3860 1.3860]

Both AEGISS functions reproduce the definition to \(\sim\!10^{-15}\). The numbers also make the subadditivity note concrete: the spatial entropy (\(0.7439\)) strictly exceeds each per-spin entropy (\(0.6930\)) — that gap is the intra-orbital \(\alpha\)–\(\beta\) correlation the spin-resolved measure marginalises out — while staying below their sum (\(1.3860\)). Here \(H(n^\alpha) = H(n^\beta)\) because a singlet has \(n_i^\alpha = n_i^\beta\); the genuinely asymmetric per-channel case needs a spin-polarised (\(n_\alpha \neq n_\beta\)) target, which is the degenerate regime.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
AEGISS exposes a small, focused public API organized around five concerns:

Module What it does Active Space High-level pipeline and individual screening functions Configuration Frozen dataclasses for all calculation settings Initial Guess Molecule construction and mean-field calculation Wavefunction DMRG and correlated wavefunction methods Localization Orbital localization methods Utilities Plotting, orbital export, MO composition, and helper functions

docs.title: Top-level imports
docs.text:
The four configuration dataclasses are available directly from the package root:

from aegiss import DMRGConfig, EntropyConfig, ProjectionConfig, OutputConfig

All other symbols should be imported from their respective submodules.

docs.title: Active Space
docs.text: Functions for selecting active space orbitals. The high-level entry point select_aegiss runs the full pipeline; the lower-level screening functions can be called independently for custom workflows.

docs.title: select_aegiss(mol: Any, mf: Any, dmrg_config: DMRGConfig, entropy_config: EntropyConfig, projection_config: ProjectionConfig, output_config: OutputConfig) -> np.ndarray | dict[str, np.ndarray]
docs.text:
Run the full AEGISS active space selection pipeline.

Runs DMRG on the specified CAS, then filters the resulting orbitals through entropy screening and AO projection. An orbital is included in the final active space when it has been selected by both criteria. Therefore, only highly entangled orbitals are kept. These orbitals must also have significant contribution on the specified AOs.

For an unrestricted (UHF) mean-field the whole pipeline runs per spin channel: when dmrg_config.spin_soe resolves to spin-resolved the alpha and beta channels are screened on their own entropy windows, otherwise they share one spin-summed window; either way the AO projection is done per spin. The alpha and beta selections are returned split and are not reconciled into a single spatial active space -- index k denotes a different MO in each channel, so no common spatial index set is defined here.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mol Mole

Molecular geometry and basis set.

required mf SCF

Converged mean-field object.

required dmrg_config DMRGConfig

Configuration for the DMRG calculation (CAS size, bond dimension, symmetry).

required entropy_config EntropyConfig

Configuration for the entropy-based screening step.

required projection_config ProjectionConfig

Configuration for the AO projection-based screening step.

required output_config OutputConfig

Configuration for output options (file saving, plots).

required

Returns:

Name Type Description active_indices np.ndarray of int, or dict[str, np.ndarray]

Sorted orbital indices of the selected active space. A single array for a restricted mean-field; a split {"alpha": ..., "beta": ...} mapping (kept separate, not reconciled) for an unrestricted one. When no orbital passes the entropy screening, an empty flat np.ndarray is returned, also for an unrestricted reference.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If an entry of projection_config.ao_labels matches no AO of the projection basis. This is checked before the DMRG run.

Source code in src/aegiss/active_space/aegiss.py 
def select_aegiss(
    mol: Any,
    mf: Any,
    dmrg_config: DMRGConfig,
    entropy_config: EntropyConfig,
    projection_config: ProjectionConfig,
    output_config: OutputConfig,
) -> np.ndarray | dict[str, np.ndarray]:
    """Run the full AEGISS active space selection pipeline.

    Runs DMRG on the specified CAS, then filters the resulting orbitals
    through entropy screening and AO projection.  An orbital is included
    in the final active space when it has been selected by *both* criteria.
    Therefore, only highly entangled orbitals are kept. These orbitals
    must also have significant contribution on the specified AOs.

    For an unrestricted (UHF) mean-field the whole pipeline runs per spin
    channel: when ``dmrg_config.spin_soe`` resolves to spin-resolved the alpha
    and beta channels are screened on their own entropy windows, otherwise they
    share one spin-summed window; either way the AO projection is done per spin.
    The alpha and beta selections are returned split and are **not** reconciled
    into a single spatial active space -- index *k* denotes a different MO in
    each channel, so no common spatial index set is defined here.

    Args:
        mol (pyscf.gto.Mole): Molecular geometry and basis set.
        mf (pyscf.scf.hf.SCF): Converged mean-field object.
        dmrg_config (DMRGConfig): Configuration for the DMRG calculation (CAS size, bond dimension, symmetry).
        entropy_config (EntropyConfig): Configuration for the entropy-based screening step.
        projection_config (ProjectionConfig): Configuration for the AO projection-based screening step.
        output_config (OutputConfig): Configuration for output options (file saving, plots).

    Returns:
        active_indices (np.ndarray of int, or dict[str, np.ndarray]): Sorted
            orbital indices of the selected active space. A single array for a
            restricted mean-field; a split ``{"alpha": ..., "beta": ...}``
            mapping (kept separate, not reconciled) for an unrestricted one.
            When no orbital passes the entropy screening, an empty flat
            ``np.ndarray`` is returned, also for an unrestricted reference.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If an entry of ``projection_config.ao_labels`` matches no AO
            of the projection basis. This is checked before the DMRG run.
    """
    _check_ao_labels(mf.mol, projection_config.ao_labels, projection_config.basis)
    active_orbs, virt_orbs = get_subspaces_from_cas(
        mf, ncas=dmrg_config.ncas, nelecas=dmrg_config.nelecas
    )
    spin_resolved = dmrg_config.spin_resolved()
    _energy, soe1 = run_dmrg_subprocess(
        mf,
        ncas=dmrg_config.ncas,
        nelecas=dmrg_config.nelecas,
        symm_type=dmrg_config.symm_type,
        max_bond_dim=dmrg_config.max_bond_dim,
        verbosity=dmrg_config.verbosity,
        unrestricted=dmrg_config.unrestricted,
        reorder=dmrg_config.reorder,
        spin_resolved=spin_resolved,
    )
    _maybe_plot_soe(output_config, active_orbs, virt_orbs, soe1)

    screened = _screen_by_entropy(
        entropy_config,
        active_orbs,
        virt_orbs,
        soe1,
        spin_resolved=spin_resolved,
    )
    if _screening_empty(screened):
        logger.info(
            "No orbitals passed the entropy screening step. Consider adjusting the "
            "EntropyConfig.fraction or using 'global' ranking for a more inclusive selection."
        )
        return np.array([], dtype=int)

    if output_config.save_orb:
        _save_entropy_orbitals(mol, mf, screened, output_config)

    base_path = (
        str(Path(output_config.saving_folder) / output_config.saving_prefix)
        if output_config.save_plots
        else None
    )
    logger.info(
        "Ranking orbitals for AO projection based on %s contribution.",
        projection_config.ranking,
    )
    passes = _ao_projection_passes(screened, projection_config.ranking)
    active_indices = _collect_active_indices(mf, projection_config, passes, base_path)

    if output_config.save_orb:
        _save_active_orbitals(mol, mf, active_indices, output_config)
    if output_config.save_plots:
        _plot_active(mol, mf, active_indices, projection_config, output_config)

    return active_indices

docs.title: select_by_entropy(occ_orbs: np.ndarray, virt_orbs: np.ndarray, soe1: np.ndarray | None, fraction: float = 0.1, fraction_type: Literal['r', 'a'] = 'r', ranking: Literal['global', 'subset'] = 'global') -> tuple[list[tuple[int, float]], list[tuple[int, float]]]

def select_by_entropy(
    occ_orbs: np.ndarray,
    virt_orbs: np.ndarray,
    soe1: np.ndarray | None,
    fraction: float = 0.1,
    fraction_type: Literal["r", "a"] = "r",
    ranking: Literal["global", "subset"] = "global",
) -> tuple[list[tuple[int, float]], list[tuple[int, float]]]:
    """Select active orbitals by single-orbital entanglement entropy.

    Args:
        occ_orbs (np.ndarray, shape (n_occ,)): Indices of occupied orbitals.
        virt_orbs (np.ndarray, shape (n_virt,)): Indices of virtual orbitals.
        soe1 (np.ndarray, shape (n_occ + n_virt,)): Single-orbital entropies for all orbitals.
        fraction (float, optional): Threshold on the entropy value. Interpretation depends on *fraction_type*.
        fraction_type ({'r', 'a'}, optional): ``'r'`` normalises entropy values by the maximum before thresholding;
            ``'a'`` applies *fraction* as an absolute threshold.
        ranking ({'global', 'subset'}, optional): ``'global'`` ranks all orbitals together; ``'subset'`` ranks occupied
            and virtual subspaces separately.

    Returns:
        selected_occ (list of tuple[int, float]): Selected occupied orbitals with entropy values.
        selected_virt (list of tuple[int, float]): Selected virtual orbitals with entropy values.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If *soe1* is not 1-D (e.g. a spin-resolved ``(2, ncas)``
            array; use :func:`select_by_spin_entropy` for that).
    """
    logger.info("----------------Entropy Screening for AEGISS----------------\n")
    if soe1 is None:
        logger.info("No single-orbital entropies provided. Returning empty selection.")
        return [], []
    if np.ndim(soe1) != 1:
        msg = (
            "select_by_entropy expects a 1-D (spin-summed) single-orbital entropy "
            f"array; got shape {np.shape(soe1)}. Spin-resolved (2, ncas) entropies "
            "must be screened per channel with select_by_spin_entropy (the alpha "
            "and beta channels are thresholded independently)."
        )
        raise ValueError(msg)
    if ranking == "global":
        logger.info("Using global ranking of orbitals by entropy values.")
        selected_occ, selected_virt = _global_entropy_ranking(
            soe1, fraction_type, fraction, occ_orbs, virt_orbs
        )
    else:
        logger.info(
            "Using relative ranking of orbitals by entropy values within the subspace."
        )
        n_occ = len(occ_orbs)
        selected_occ = _relative_entropy_ranking(
            soe1[:n_occ], fraction_type, fraction, occ_orbs
        )
        selected_virt = _relative_entropy_ranking(
            soe1[n_occ:], fraction_type, fraction, virt_orbs
        )

    for i in selected_occ:
        logger.info(
            "\tSelected occupied orbital %d: S(1) = %.4f", to_display(i[0]), i[1]
        )
    for i in selected_virt:
        logger.info(
            "\tSelected virtual orbital %d:  S(1) = %.4f", to_display(i[0]), i[1]
        )

    return selected_occ, selected_virt

def select_by_spin_entropy(
    occ_orbs: np.ndarray,
    virt_orbs: np.ndarray,
    soe1: np.ndarray | None,
    fraction: float = 0.1,
    fraction_type: Literal["r", "a"] = "r",
    ranking: Literal["global", "subset"] = "global",
) -> dict[str, tuple[list[tuple[int, float]], list[tuple[int, float]]]]:
    """Screen the alpha and beta channels independently from a spin-resolved SOE.

    For a spin-polarised target the single spin-orbital entropies
    ``H(n_alpha)`` and ``H(n_beta)`` differ between channels (e.g. an open-shell
    SOMO is entangled in one spin channel and frozen in the other), so each
    channel is thresholded on its own. This yields a *split* selection: the alpha
    and beta active windows may contain different orbitals.

    Args:
        occ_orbs (np.ndarray): Occupied orbital indices of the screening window
            (shared by both spin channels; the split is in which of them each
            channel keeps).
        virt_orbs (np.ndarray): Virtual orbital indices of the screening window.
        soe1 (np.ndarray, shape (2, n_occ + n_virt)): Spin-resolved single
            spin-orbital entropies (row 0 = alpha, row 1 = beta), as returned by
            ``run_dmrg_subprocess(..., spin_resolved=True)``. ``None`` returns
            an empty selection for both channels.
        fraction (float, optional): Same meaning as in :func:`select_by_entropy`;
            a single value is used for both channels.
        fraction_type ({'r', 'a'}, optional): Same meaning as in
            :func:`select_by_entropy`.
        ranking ({'global', 'subset'}, optional): Same meaning as in
            :func:`select_by_entropy`; applied to each channel independently.

    Returns:
        selection (dict[str, tuple[list, list]]): ``{"alpha": (occ_alpha,
            virt_alpha), "beta": (occ_beta, virt_beta)}``, each entry an
            ``(index, entropy)`` list as from :func:`select_by_entropy`.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If *soe1* is not a ``(2, ncas)`` array.
    """
    if soe1 is None:
        logger.info("No single-orbital entropies provided. Returning empty selection.")
        return {"alpha": ([], []), "beta": ([], [])}
    soe = np.asarray(soe1, dtype=float)
    if soe.ndim != 2 or soe.shape[0] != 2:
        msg = (
            "select_by_spin_entropy expects a spin-resolved (2, ncas) SOE array "
            f"(row 0 = alpha, row 1 = beta); got shape {soe.shape}. For a "
            "spin-summed 1-D array use select_by_entropy."
        )
        raise ValueError(msg)

    selection: dict[str, tuple[list[tuple[int, float]], list[tuple[int, float]]]] = {}
    for spin, channel in enumerate(("alpha", "beta")):
        logger.info("=============== %s channel ===============", channel.upper())
        selection[channel] = select_by_entropy(
            occ_orbs=occ_orbs,
            virt_orbs=virt_orbs,
            soe1=soe[spin],
            fraction=fraction,
            fraction_type=fraction_type,
            ranking=ranking,
        )
    return selection

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mf SCF or KohnShamDFT

Mean-field object containing the molecular orbitals and occupation numbers.

A single float applies to all AO groups; a list specifies per-group thresholds and should match the length of ao_labels; on a length mismatch a warning is logged and the first value is used for every group. A non-dict value is shared by both channels. A dict is rejected for a restricted mean-field.

For an unrestricted mean-field it may also be a spin-resolved {"alpha": ..., "beta": ...} mapping (as produced by select_by_spin_entropy), in which case each spin channel is restricted to its own space.
